questions.question: What is the 'golden rule' for choosing between multiple coding rules that seem to fit?
options: Always pick the most complex rule
Always prefer the SIMPLEST rule that remains consistent across every given example, not just some of them
Pick a rule at random
Prefer whichever rule was thought of first
questions.rationale: The golden rule is to always prefer the simplest rule that holds true across every given example, rather than a more complex one that only partially fits.

questions.question: What does 'rule verification' require before finalizing an answer?
options: Checking only the first letter
Confirming the candidate rule correctly explains every part of every given example, not just the first one checked
Skipping verification to save time
Only verifying if the rule seems complex
questions.rationale: Full rule verification means confirming the candidate rule correctly accounts for every part of every given example, not stopping after a single partial check.

questions.question: Why is 'two-example verification' (when two examples are given) especially valuable?
options: It is no more valuable than one example
A rule that holds across two independent examples is far less likely to be a coincidence than one based on a single example
It replaces the need for any verification
It only matters for number coding
questions.rationale: A rule confirmed across two independent examples is much more reliable, since coincidentally fitting one example is far more likely than coincidentally fitting two.

questions.question: What does 'contradiction detection' catch during coding rule verification?
options: Nothing useful
A candidate rule that works for one part of an example but produces a wrong result for another part, revealing it's not the correct rule
Only spelling errors
Only errors in the final answer choice
questions.rationale: Contradiction detection catches cases where a candidate rule explains one part of an example correctly but fails on another part, revealing that it isn't actually the correct rule.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a formal 'coding solving algorithm'?
options: To make solving slower and more complex
To provide a repeatable, systematic sequence of steps for identifying and verifying a coding rule, rather than guessing
To replace the need for any examples
To only apply to letter-shift coding
questions.rationale: A formal solving algorithm provides a repeatable, systematic sequence of steps for identifying and verifying the correct coding rule, rather than relying on guesswork.

questions.question: What does a 'master solving flowchart' consolidate?
options: Only the golden rule
The full decision process for identifying, testing, and applying the correct coding rule, laid out as a step-by-step flowchart
Only the wrap-around rule
A random selection of examples
questions.rationale: A master solving flowchart lays out the complete decision process — identifying, testing, and applying the rule — as a clear, step-by-step visual guide.

questions.question: What does 'pairwise operations' (an advanced pattern) apply an operation to?
options: Each individual letter separately
Pairs of adjacent letters or numbers, rather than to each individual one separately
Only the first and last letters
The word's total length
questions.rationale: Pairwise operations apply a transformation to pairs of adjacent letters or numbers together, rather than treating each one in isolation.

questions.question: What does 'pair sum coding' compute?
options: The individual position of each letter
The sum of each pair of adjacent letters' (or numbers') position values
The word's total length
The product of all letters combined
questions.rationale: Pair sum coding computes the sum of each pair of adjacent letters' or numbers' values, working through the word pair by pair.

questions.question: What does 'pair difference coding' compute, in contrast?
options: The same sum as pair sum coding
The difference between each pair of adjacent letters' (or numbers') position values
The word's total length
The average value of the whole word
questions.rationale: Pair difference coding computes the numeric gap between each pair of adjacent letters' or numbers' values, rather than their sum.

questions.question: Why must the simplest-consistent-rule principle always be checked against ALL given data, not just convenient parts of it?
options: Partial checking is always sufficient
Because a rule that only explains part of the data isn't actually verified — it might coincidentally match a subset while being wrong overall
Because all data is always identical
Because this principle only applies to number coding
questions.rationale: A rule that only explains part of the data hasn't truly been verified — it may coincidentally fit that subset while actually being incorrect when checked against everything given.
